public_rationale: The Abilene disclosures identify outside capital partners funding infrastructure used by OpenAI. They are material counterevidence to a literal claim that every funding dollar came from hyperscalers. But the same project involves Oracle, and the records do not settle whether Zitron means project capital or the economic commitments underwriting it. A categorical score would therefore depend on a financing interpretation he did not specify. His hedged $250 billion estimate is not treated as an exact realized-cost promise.
limitations: The project evidence does not measure the combined historical infrastructure costs of both labs.
Outside financing does not by itself establish who ultimately bears the infrastructure cost.
The beginning of the historical interval is unspecified.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: OpenAI's and Anthropic's infrastructure costs were entirely funded by hyperscalers, likely about $250 billion on top of nearly $300 billion they raised.

statement.excerpt: While OpenAI and Anthropic have raised nearly $300 billion in the last few years, their actual infrastructure costs — the GPUs and the data centers to power their services — were entirely funded by hyperscalers, likely costing another $250 billion in the process

from_speaker: raised nearly $300 billion in the last few years
the GPUs and the data centers to power their services
Microsoft has said it spent $100 billion on its OpenAI relationship as of early 2026
our_interpretation: The firm assertion is that hyperscalers supplied all funding for the physical infrastructure serving the two labs.
The plain reading distinguishes funding that infrastructure from raising equity for the labs. It does not automatically equate paying a cloud-service invoice with financing construction.
The $250 billion figure is explicitly an estimate. Establishing that exact realized total is not a condition for supporting the categorical funding assertion.
The nearly $300 billion raised and Microsoft's reported spending are premises, not amounts that may simply be added to produce an infrastructure total.
The historical interval ends at publication. Its start remains unspecified because last few years does not establish a particular year.
Oracle is not excluded merely because it is smaller than the three providers named later. CoreWeave's classification and the treatment of outside capital providers remain explicit ambiguities.
criteria.support_condition: Records covering the relevant infrastructure establish that hyperscalers supplied its funding throughout the described period, with no material independent infrastructure funding. The hedged $250 billion estimate need not equal an audited total.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Records identify infrastructure actually serving either lab that was independently funded outside the hyperscaler group, with enough information to distinguish independent funding from a hyperscaler's borrowing, lease obligations or financing arrangements. A cloud invoice or an unidentified lender alone is insufficient.

evidence.locator: Statement by Crusoe CEO Chase Lochmiller
evidence.explanation: Crusoe identifies outside capital partnerships for the $15 billion Abilene joint venture. This challenges a literal all-capital-from-hyperscalers reading, but does not establish how funding obligations should be attributed after accounting for the tenant's commitments.

evidence.locator: Paragraph beginning Meanwhile, construction of Stargate I
evidence.explanation: OpenAI identifies Abilene as an operating Stargate site and describes training and inference using Oracle-delivered equipment. This connects the project in e3 to OpenAI, while also showing why Oracle's role cannot be ignored when interpreting who funded it.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Project-level records identifying capital contributions, tenant guarantees and payment obligations for infrastructure serving both labs, with an explicit and consistently applied meaning of funded and hyperscaler.
